57 Petersham Road Feb. 23, '40.

Yours of Feb. 18 to hand this A.M.

Re partners. Most important never to divulge your business. They never understand. But I think all payments to G.M.C. should be credited to your O.T.O. interests esp. in California where both Smith and Mas S. have acquired-properties, which will be very useful for your vieuz jours (and mine, if I can ever get out there!) I want very much to go over and devlop these. As soon as I can do so, I can put the O.T.O. really on its feet again; for my presence and personality and literary & dramatic connexions should enable me to conquer Hollywood. (I can't send photos of the properties because of the censor. But they look very promising.) ---

Newton has been away ill. I see him Monday, I hope. He has capitalists in Belgium. So if I can talk him into it, you might be able to explain your proposition to the man on the spot, and start immediately. ---

I'm in trouble here. My Trust Fund has got cold feet, so that I can't count on my weekly £2. I had to put your cheque through in consequence. Normally, though, I'm quite o.k. personally. But in order to push the Tarot I shall have to renew my wardrobe, at least one suit, amd some underclothes. This will cost about £30. Then, of course, the printer. I shall probably have to be content with a one-page war poem for March 21. But please remember that even the smallest cheque makes all the difference between staying idle and dashing about to put business through.

P.S. Sorry if this letter seems gloomy. But I have been rather sick, and still don't feel too gay. I'm worried about the Tarot: we are so near to the end - and it's the biggest work of my whole life - that I can't help wondering if some 'tuile' isn't going to drop! I suppose that's liver too.

units.text: In this lesson, we explore the foundations of financial instability as experienced by the writer during a critical period.
The source material comes from a letter dated 23rd February 1940, where he discusses his financial troubles and their impact on his Tarot project.
First, the writer reveals that his trust fund had become unreliable.
He says, My trust fund has got cold feet so that I can't count on my weekly.
This meant he could no longer rely on a steady income from that source.
He adds that he had to put a check through in consequence, indicating he was forced to use other funds to cover his needs.
Second, he emphasizes how even a small check could make a significant difference.
He writes, Even the smallest check makes all the difference between staying idle and dashing about to put business through.
In other words, a modest influx of funds could shift him from inaction to actively pursuing his goals.
Third, the financial need for the Tarot project is apparent.
He states he is worried about the Tarot and calls it the biggest work of my whole life.
To push it forward, he says, I shall have to renew my wardrobe at least one suit and some underclothes.
This will cost about 30 pounds, then of course the printer.
These specific expenses highlight the financial requirements for completing and promoting the Tarot.
To recapat, the writer faced financial instability because his trust fund became unreliable.
He stressed that even a small check could make the difference between idleness and active work.
Finally, he detailed the financial needs for his Tarot project, including wardrobe and printing costs.
These factors combine to create a foundation of financial uncertainty during this period.

This session draws on a letter written by Aleister Crowley.
In it he speaks directly about the tarot project that consumed him.
The tarot was the biggest work of his whole life.
He says that plainly, it's the biggest work of my whole life.
Not just a big project, but the biggest.
That is the scale he assigned to it.
Yet he was deeply worried about its completion.
He writes, I'm worried about the tarot.
We are so near to the end.
And it's the biggest work of my whole life that I can't help wondering if some trick isn't going to drop.
He feared that some last minute obstacle, some trick, would prevent the work from being finished.
He even wondered if his worry was simply due to feeling unwell.
I suppose that's liver too.
But the anxiety was real.
To push the tarot through, he needed practical things specifically.
In order to push the tarot, I shall have to renew my wardrobe, at least one suit and some underclothes.
This will cost about thirty pounds.
Then of course, the printer.
So two concrete needs, a new set of clothes to present himself properly, and a printer to produce the actual deck or book.
To recap, the tarot was Crowley's magnum opus, the biggest work of his life.
He was worried it might be sabotaged, just as it neared the end, and he required both a refreshed wardrobe and a printer to bring it to completion.
These are the only facts about this project that appear in the source material.
